item.title: REVIEW: Amazon Echo Glow Review
item.description:
Source: PCMag
This is the most recent version of the Echo Glow. Read our review from January 2, 2020 below. The Amazon Echo Glow ($29.99) is a kid-friendly smart light that cycles through 16 colors with a tap of your hand. This smallish orb-shaped lamp is easy to get up and running, works with Amazon's FreeTime service, and can be programmed to follow Alexa routines that allow it to interact with other Alexa-enabled products. That said, you'll need a separate Alexa device to control the Glow with your voice as it lacks a speaker and microphone, and it's not bright enough to be used for anything other than mood lighting or a colorful night-light. About the size of a softball, the Glow is a round white LED lamp with a flat base and a frosted white light lens. It measures 3.9 inches around and has a hardwired USB power cord and an Action button. The Glow can display 16 colors including a warmish white (2600K) and variations of blue, green, orange, red, and yellow. It even has a salmon color. The dimmable bulb only puts out 100 lumens, which is fine for use as a night-light or for subtle mood lighting effects, but not nearly bright enough to illuminate a room. There are several ways to change colors; through the mobile app, with Alexa voice commands (if you connect it to another Echo device with a microphone), and using Alexa routines. You can also simply tap the lens—each time you tap it, the Glow will cycle through to the next color in the palette. Despite its name, the Echo Glow isn't an Echo speaker. You can control it with the Alexa app, but it doesn't have a microphone, and even if it did, it lacks the technology that allows you to control it directly with your voice. However, it does have a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi radio that lets you connect it to an Echo speaker or other Alexa-enabled device so you can control it using voice commands. The lamp supports the kid-friendly FreeTime subscription service, and it offers a Rainbow Timer that uses colors to help motivate kids to complete tasks like homework or brushing their teeth on time. It also supports Alexa Routines that allow it to integrate with other smart home devices that are linked to your Alexa account including indoor/outdoor cameras, thermostats, and video doorbells. Apple HomeKit, Google Assistant, and IFTTT applets aren't supported, however. The Glow uses the same Alexa app all other Alexa devices. When you launch the app, tap Devices at the bottom of the screen, tap Lights, then tap the tab with the name of your Glow lamp. This opens a screen with an on/off button, a brightness slider, a Color tab, a Mode tab, and a button labeled Create A Routine. Tap the Set button on the Color tab to select a color and tap the Mode button to select a lighting effect including Campfire, Color Flow, Disco, Firetruck, Mood Light, Siren, and Underwater. There are also seasonal lighting effects for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa, and Valentine's Day, as well as a Solid Color choice. Tap the Create A Routine button to create schedules, have the Glow react to your phone's location, and to make it work with other smart home devices that are linked to your Alexa. In the upper right corner is a gear icon that opens a settings screen where you can change Wi-Fi settings, view firmware information, and disable the light. The Echo Glow is easy to install, but you'll have to download the Alexa app and create an account if you don't already have one. I plugged the Glow into a power outlet, opened the app, and tapped Devices in the lower right corner. I then tapped the plus icon to add a device, selected Light, then selected Amazon Echo. I used my phone's camera to scan the QR code on the bottom of the device, and the app automatically connected the Glow to the same Wi-Fi network used by my phone. The Glow was connected immediately and I was given the option of adding it to a group or skipping this step. I gave the light a name and came to a screen that required me to enter my Amazon password and the CVV code from the credit card associated with my account (there are no charges to your card, but this information is required to prove you're an adult). Next, I was presented with a Parental Consent agreement that lets you use the Glow as part of Amazon's kid's services such FreeTime. By agreeing to this, you're allowing Amazon to collect information about your child or children including their name, birthday, and email address. This also gives Amazon permission to access your child's photos, videos, and location information. Once I agreed to the above terms, the Glow installation was complete. The light delivered nice soft colors in testing, but as previously mentioned, it's not very bright. That said, cycling through the color palette using tap control is easy, as is changing colors and brightness levels using Alexa voice commands and the mobile app. The lighting Modes worked nicely; I particularly like the Campfire and Color Flow effects. I created an Alexa routine to have the Glow turn on daily in the afternoon with the color set to blue and it followed this routine without fail. It also had no trouble following my Alexa routine to have the Glow turn on with a red color whenever an Arlo Pro 3 camera detected motion. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. item.title: REVIEW: ‘Marvel’s Wolverine’ Was a Disappointment
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
This week, I finally finished Marvel’s Wolverine. I kind of had to. With a brand new copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake staring me in the face, and a download code for Grand Theft Auto VI on the way, I wanted to at least see how the game I’d been struggling to get through ended before moving on to other things. “Struggling” not because the game was particularly challenging in any way, though it could be at times. No, I was “struggling” because it took me forever to find any meaningful attachment to it. And, while I’m ultimately glad I did get to the end, it was quite the journey to get there. So let’s jump back to the beginning. I, like many of you, was incredibly excited when I heard that Insomniac Games, the same team behind probably my favorite superhero games of all time, the Spider-Man games, was doing a Wolverine game. I’ve loved Wolverine since the first time I saw that devilish haircut and those shiny claws on a comic book shelf in the late 1980s. Over the years, I’ve bought his comics, his toys, his cards. When I first saw him on the big screen, it was so magical, it was almost difficult to comprehend. Even playing as him in the classic X-Men arcade game was something I was very much into. So a Wolverine game from the Spider-Man team? How lucky were we? After years of waiting, when the game was finally released, I dove right in. My colleague, Justin Carter, reviewed the game for io9 and liked it, so I was encouraged. But pretty quickly, things didn’t sit well with me. The first thing that hit me was that there was no big, sprawling, open world like in Spider-Man. I hadn’t read too much about the game in the lead-up, so I probably should have known that, but it was still a bummer. Instead, this was a much more straightforward, linear game which, honestly, lent itself better to this story. So while I wasn’t super happy about the choice, I quickly embraced it. After a few minutes, though, something else felt wrong: my hand. I realized I had been smashing the square button on my controller an awful lot. Maybe too much. As the game went on, various alternate moves and combinations emerged, offering some welcome variety but, for the most part, it was button smashing over everything else. Everything in the game also felt repetitive and slightly lazy. You’re fighting a bunch of Reavers. Now you’re fighting The Hand. Now it’s the Reavers again, but with bigger guns. We’re in Japan. We’re in Madripoor. Then we’re in Japan again. Then Madripoor again. Hightown, Lowtown, get the Engine, lose the Engine, get the Engine again, etc. And often pieces of the story were conveyed because characters recorded themselves on handheld devices and just left them sitting around for no apparent reason. There were some undeniable pluses, though. Like that it’s incredibly fun to slice and dice as Wolverine. The performances of the actors, the graphics, and the insanely gross and satisfying violence helped keep things exciting. Having a little love story at the center with Jean Grey was nice too. Eventually, as the story very, very slowly got to the very, very obvious reveal of the true villain, I actually found myself enjoying it more and more. The third act, in particular, has a lot of big, memorable moments that led me to believe I was almost done with the game. I was not. If I were enjoying the game a little bit more or curious about what happened next, the fact that it all felt so drawn out probably would’ve been okay. I’ve played games or watched movies I’ve never wanted to end. And I’ve played games and watched movies that couldn’t end fast enough. Wolverine felt like the latter. Part of that is because the game doesn’t find a way to comfortably integrate this deep, layered past it’s created for Wolverine alongside the main story. You have to veer off the path of the main game and complete seemingly unrelated tasks to get tiny hints about the character. And while that long, arduous task does ultimately have a satisfying conclusion, I can also imagine players skipping those side quests in favor of continuing to kill the non-stop parade of bad guys. However, you have to complete those side quests to get to the game’s biggest reveal: it’s not just a game about mutant survival. It’s a love story for the ages, something that’s very loosely seeded throughout and only revealed in full at the end. By that point, though, you’re done playing, so it loses some of the emotional impact it was clearly meant to have. And so, after 18 hours spread across several weeks (a few of which, to be fair, I was travelling during), I finally finished the game. I’m glad I did. There’s enough good stuff in there to warrant a play-through, especially if stabbing and chopping off heads with adamantium claws is your thing. But the fact that finishing the game felt more like a chore than a privilege was a disappointment. Want more io9 news? item.title: SALES: The 16GB Pi 5 costs almost $400, here's the mini PC you should buy instead
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
The Raspberry Pi just got a massive price hike. You'll now have to spend around $500 to get a full Pi 5 16GB setup, which is just crazy to me. I really don't think the Pi 5 is worth it at that price, as you can do almost everything that a Pi can do with a mini PC (outside of GPIO pins). So, if you're considering buying a 16GB Raspberry Pi 5, let me try and convince you otherwise by showing you that a mini PC is more upgradable and better suited for your homelab. It launched at $120 less than two years ago For well over a decade now, the Raspberry Pi has been known as an affordable single-board computer for a wide range of tasks. Based on an Arm processor, it doesn’t necessarily run Windows all that well, but it’s the perfect mini system for those who like running Linux. I’ve known multiple people who ran a Raspberry Pi as their main computer because it was just cheap and it worked well. It used to be that Raspberry Pis only came as low-spec systems. The Pi 3 B that I have only has 1GB of RAM, for example. However, less than two years ago in January 2025, Raspberry Pi launched a 16GB Pi 5 for $120. It was one of the most expensive Pi systems ever released at the time, but it finally made the Pi a feasible computer for people who needed more power than the cheaper systems offered. On November 2, 2026, Raspberry Pi announced that the Pi 5 16GB was getting yet another price increase—this time to $385. That’s over three times the price of what it launched at less than 24 months ago, and the actual Pi itself hasn’t changed. It’s still the same 16GB Pi 5 that was launched at the beginning of 2025, but Raspberry Pi blames the price increase on the DRAM supply and hopes to roll it back in price at some point, but doesn’t know if or when it will happen. A $385 Pi still needs about $100 more before it boots from an SSD Power, cooling and an M.2 HAT aren't optional at this tier So, for $385, you get a fully-working computer ready to use right out of the box, right? Wrong. For $385, you get just the Pi 5 16GB unit itself. You’ll need a power supply, which costs another $12. Most people will want an active cooler to keep performance up, which is another $5. Oh, and the Pi 5 doesn’t come with storage at all, so you’ll have to supply that yourself—and a 512GB SSD that's compatible with the Pi costs over $100. The Pi 5 only ships with the ability to use MicroSD from the factory, which you’ll have to buy yourself. If you want to use it with an NVMe drive, then you’ll need to buy a separate adapter which is another $12 plus an SSD to use it with. All of this adds up to over $100 extra just to get the Pi 5 into working order for you to use as a computer, putting you close to, if not over $500 for a fully-working Pi 5 16GB when all’s said and done. An N150 box with 16GB lands under $400 all-in, storage included So, if a Raspberry Pi 16GB costs $385 without storage or other necessary accessories, and more than $500 once you buy everything else, what mini PC should you get instead? It all depends on the hardware you need. For $399—just $14 more than a Raspberry Pi—you can get a mini PC with Intel's N150 processor, 16GB of user-upgradable DDR4 RAM, a 500GB NVMe drive (with room for a second NVMe drive if you need), and Windows 11 Pro pre-installed. If you go up to $500, you can get a mini PC that sports the Intel i7-1185G7 processor with Iris Xe graphics, 16GB of user-upgradable DDR4 RAM, 2.5Gb Ethernet, a 512GB NVMe drive (with room for a second), and Windows 11 Pro pre-installed. Really, there are a ton of great systems you can buy for the same price as a 16GB Raspberry Pi 5, and very few reasons to spend the cash on buying a Raspberry Pi 5 at this price point. There's even a mini PC with dual Gigabit Ethernet for just over $400.

With the Core 3 304 processor and 12GB of LPDDR5X RAM, this tiny desktop offers Wi-Fi 7, dual RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet, and support for up to three 4K displays. See at Amazon $490 at BOSGAME Why buy a mini PC over a Raspberry Pi? Well, a mini PC is based on the x86 architecture instead of Arm, which makes it more compatible with most services. For instance, Plex doesn't support native hardware transcoding on a Raspberry Pi, while it does support the Intel processors in mini PCs. You can also still install Linux on just about any mini PC you buy, while you can't really install Windows on a Raspberry Pi. Also, as I mentioned above, you can upgrade the RAM in most mini PCs, meaning you could buy a smaller amount like 8GB or 16GB now, and upgrade it with more RAM in the future if you need. Plus, mini PCs typically support at least two storage drives, making it easier to add extra room for games or documents compared to trying to upgrade a Raspberry Pi. The Pi is still the right buy for pin projects I'm not saying the Raspberry Pi 5 is a bad system—it's still great. I just wouldn't go spend $385 plus extras to get a Raspberry Pi. If you want to run Linux, buy a mini PC and install Linux on it. If you need GPIO pins, you probably don't need 16GB of RAM. All Pi 5 models ship with the same quad-core Cortex-A76 SoC and 40-pin GPIO, meaning every Pi 5 has the same capabilities except how much RAM it has. So, before you drop $500 or more on setting up a Pi 5 16GB, really weigh if your Pi 5 project needs 16GB of RAM. Chances are it doesn't. If it does, then double check that a mini PC wouldn't be the better option for your needs instead. I still don't know why Raspberry Pis are so expensive these days Raspberry Pi says that they keep raising the price due to DRAM costs. I understand that RAM is getting more expensive in the age of AI everything, but if a mini PC, with way more ports and capabilities than a Raspberry Pi, can stay affordable, why can't the Pi itself? It just doesn't make sense to me. Mini PCs haven't gone up all that much in price with the RAM price hikes. You can find some mini PCs in the sub-$300 range with solid specs. Yet, for some reason, Raspberry Pi is hiking the price for its systems multiple times in a year to unaffordable new heights. Unless you need the capabilities of a Raspberry Pi, just get a mini PC. It's better supported with the software you'll likely run in your homelab, and it's just simply more affordable and upgradable at this point.

item.title: SALES: Best gaming monitors 2026: Displays that will do your games justice
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Any monitor can be used for PC gaming, but a display built for productivity will likely leave you feeling less than satisfied. Limited contrast, blurry motion, and slow refresh rates still hold back the performance of basic productivity monitors in games. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of excellent gaming monitors available at a range of budgets—and the best of them embrace cutting-edge technology unavailable in any other PC display. Below are our picks of the best gaming monitors we’ve tested throughout this year and last. If you want to learn more about what we look for in a good gaming monitor and how we test them, scroll further down the page. Why you should trust PCWorld for monitors reviews and buying advice: We’re PCWorld, after all. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review dozens of monitors every year. All of our recommendations have been personally tested and vetted by our expert reviewers, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. - Gamma, color temperature slightly off-target Who should buy the MSI MPG 272URX QD-OLED? If you’re looking for a high-performance gaming monitor, the MSI MPG 272URX QD-OLED should be at the top of your list. This 26.5-inch display delivers stunning 4K resolution with an ultra-smooth 240Hz refresh rate in a cutting-edge OLED panel, making it an excellent choice for gamers who want both visual clarity and fluid motion. With its 240Hz refresh rate, the MSI is built for fast-paced gaming yet maintains the deep contrast and vibrant colors OLED monitors are known for. It also supports Adaptive Sync for smooth frame pacing. MSI MPG 272URX QD-OLED: Further considerations But wait, there’s more! The QD-OLED panel offers excellent contrast and color accuracy, which makes it a solid pick for creative professionals and anyone who enjoys watching HDR movies. Connectivity is another plus, with HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 2.1a, and USB-C inputs, as well as 98 watts of USB Power Delivery for charging laptops or tablets. While the design is a bit plain, the stand is sturdy and fully adjustable. Priced at $1,099.99, the MSI MPG 272URX is more expensive than 1440p OLED alternatives, which can be found for under $800. But if 4K clarity and a fluid 240Hz refresh rate are what you’re after, this monitor is worth the investment. Pixio PX248 Wave – Best budget gaming monitor - Attractive design, especially in unique colorways - Built-in speakers are surprisingly decent - Solid color accuracy and respectable gamut Who should buy the Pixio PX248 Wave? The Pixio PX248 Wave is a great budget monitor for gamers who want more than a no-frills display. The PX248 Wave stands apart from the budget pack with a colorful, stylish design, and solid motion performance, all available at an enticing price of $159.99. Pixio offers the PX248 Wave in four colorways: black, white, blue, and pink. The latter two are rather special, as only a handful of monitors — like the more expensive Samsung M8 Smart Monitor — offer similarly alluring colors. The stand matches the monitor’s colorway, and Pixio even offers an optional color-coordinated monitor arm for those who want to go all-in on a particular desktop vibe. The monitor’s 24-inch Fast IPS display boasts a 200Hz refresh rate that delivers fluid motion. Image quality is reasonable, too, as the PX248 Wave delivers respectable color accuracy and coverage, making it suitable for both gaming and casual content creation. It has built-in speakers, too. Pixio PX248 Wave: Further considerations Despite its visual appeal, the PX248 Wave sticks to the basics with connectivity, which includes HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort 1.4. USB connectivity isn’t available. The included stand is also basic, as it only adjusts for tilt, and the menu controls could be more user-friendly. Most competitors at this price point have a similar display panel wrapped in a more generic black, gray, or charcoal case. Pixio’s PX248 Wave manages to match them in image quality and beat them on looks, yet it stays on a budget. LG Ultragear 45GX950A-B – Best curved gaming monitor - Incredibly immersive 45-inch ultrawide panel - Design isn’t bad, but not up to the price tag - Curved display will be too extreme for some Who should buy the LG Ultragear 45GX950A-B? The LG Ultragear 45GX950A-B is the best big-screen curved gaming monitor for anyone who wants a premium immersive gaming experience. The monitor’s class-leading 45-inch 5K2K (5120×2160) OLED panel helps to set the monitor apart, providing a resolution previously unseen in this size class. It’s a significant upgrade over lower-resolution predecessors, like the Corsair Xeneon Flex. The higher resolution pairs well with OLED’s excellent contrast and color performance. HDR performance is solid, with brightness comparable to other leading OLED monitors. Motion clarity is good, as well. The monitor is a “dual mode” display, meaning it can achieve 5120×2160 at a refresh rate up to 165Hz, or 2560×1080 up to 330Hz. It also supports AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and Nvidia G-Sync for smooth gameplay. LG Ultragear 45GX950A-B: Further considerations The 45GX950A-B is expensive, and its aggressive 800R curve can feel “off” for productivity. The monitor also has limited USB connectivity. USB-C input is supported, but it only has two downstream USB-A ports. But if your priority is unparalleled immersion backed by incredible sharpness and excellent HDR on a truly massive display, the LG Ultragear 45GX950A-B is a winner. Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMG – Best HDR gaming monitor - Superb contrast with deep, inky black levels - HDMI ports don’t support 240Hz refresh rate - SDR performance is great, but slightly lags QD-OLED peers Who should buy the Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMG? If you’re searching for the best gaming monitor for HDR, look no further than the Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMG. It has an LG WOLED panel that delivers stunning HDR without breaking the bank. The XG27AQDMG’s third-generation LG WOLED panel provides exceptional HDR brightness that outperforms QD-OLED competitors and closes the gap with Mini-LED monitors. It can hit a maximum sustained brightness of 724 nits in a 10 percent window, which is enough to deliver punchy HDR highlights and detail across luminant areas of a game or movie. This pairs well with OLED’s deep, inky blacks and wide color gamut, which covers 96 percent DCI-P3 coverage. Put simply: It looks exceptionally immersive and realistic. Gamers will appreciate the high refresh rate of up to 240Hz, which is paired with Adaptive Sync technologies like AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and Nvidia G-Sync for fluid, tear-free gaming. The refresh rate is lower than some QD-OLED competitors, which achieve up to 360Hz. On the other hand, though, the XG27AQDMG provides motion clarity far better than Mini-LED gaming monitors, such as the Red Magic 4K Gaming Monitor. Asus ROG Strix XG27AQDMG: Further considerations While the XG27AQDMG has strong color performance, it isn’t quite as good as QD-OLED alternatives with SDR. Sharpness is merely okay, too, and small fonts can look pixelated at times. Pricing, however, is an upside. Sold at an MSRP of $749.99, and immediately available for just $699.99 at release, the XG27AQDMG undercuts the competition on price. Gamers who mostly stick to SDR may want to pay $50 to $100 more for a QD-OLED alternative, but the XG27AQDMG has the edge in HDR. Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27AQWP-W – Best high-refresh gaming monitor - Good SDR brightness for OLED, great contrast - Sets a new high mark for motion performance - Stand is a bit large for 27-inch display Who should buy the Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27AQWP-W? The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27AQWP-W is built for competitive gamers who prioritize motion clarity above all else. With refresh rates reaching 540Hz at 1440p and 720Hz at 720p, it delivers the best motion performance available from any display to date (which says a lot, as many high-refresh monitors have been released of late). The Extreme Low Motion Blur feature is particularly impressive, offering exceptional clarity even at lower refresh rates for games that can’t hit extreme frame rates. The monitor’s tandem OLED panel delivers great image quality with strong SDR and HDR brightness, stellar contrast, and a wide color gamut covering 99 percent of DCI-P3. The ultra-glossy TrueBlack finish maximizes perceived contrast for an incredibly rich image in darker viewing environments. Combined with features like Aura Sync RGB lighting and extensive menu customization, it’s a premium package for enthusiasts. Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27AQWP-W: Further considerations The PG27AQWP-W lacks USB-C connectivity and the ultra-glossy finish can be annoying if you have windows or bright lights nearby. The large tripod-style stand also takes up considerable desk space. It stands in contrast to recent OLED monitors from brands like MSI, which tend to include USB-C. But the most important thing to consider is just how high a refresh rate you really need. 540Hz at 1440p is amazingly crisp, to be sure, but you might find better value in a less expensive 4K OLED monitors running at 240Hz. That’s particularly true if you want to use the monitor for both work and play. Asus ROG Strix 5K XG27JCG – Best 5K gaming monitor - Functional design with a small stand base and tripod mounting - Many image-quality features and adjustments - 27-inch 5K panel looks extremely sharp - Combo of high refresh rate, ELMB Sync, and ELMB 2 deliver on motion clarity - USB-C port only provides 15 watts of power delivery - Mid-tier contrast and color performance Who should buy the Asus ROG Strix 5K XG27JCG? This 27-inch Fast IPS display delivers 5K resolution at up to 180Hz, an unusual combination that makes it ideal for gamers who want extreme pixel density without sacrificing motion clarity. At 218 pixels per inch, text and fine detail are rendered with a crispness that 4K monitors can’t match. Asus’ ELMB2 backlight strobing technology pushes motion performance further still with a CRT-like scanning technique to reduce blur dramatically. The monitor can also drop to 1440p at up to 330Hz if your GPU needs a break from pushing 5K frame rates. The monitor also tosses in a few nice extras. It has four video inputs (two HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, and USB-C) which gives it more connection flexibility than most competitors, and a handy tripod mount on the stand neck lets you attach webcam arms or ring lights cleanly. Asus ROG Strix 5K XG27JCG: Further considerations Though it has much to recommend it, the XG27JCG has a few weaknesses. The monitor tops out around 1,230:1, so dark scenes look washed out compared to OLED alternatives. The USB-C port delivers only 15 watts, which is enough to charge a phone, but not a laptop. And while it’s technically VESA DisplayHDR 600 certified, HDR quality is limited by the monitor’s edge-lit backlight design. At $849.99, the XG27JCG is just a sliver less expensive than a typical 4K OLED monitor. Many gamers will find that’s more than sharp enough. But if you want to game at absurdly high resolutions, or want outstanding motion clarity thanks to the monitor’s ELMB2 technology, the XG27JCG is worth your money. Other notable gaming monitors we’ve reviewed - KTC 27M1: A do-it-all budget monitor that’s suitable for both gaming and productivity. - Acer Predator X34 X0: A Mini-LED ultrawide for less than $500. - Alienware AW2725Q: An excellent 27-inch 4K 240Hz QD-OLED monitor, and less expensive than the competition. - BenQ PD3226G: A monitor for creative professionals, but it’s not bad in PC games, either. - Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCDM: A 27-inch 4K QD-OLED monitor delivers gorgeous image quality and a long list of features, though it certainly isn’t cheap. - MSI MPG 321URXW QD-OLED: An excellent 32-inch 4K QD-OLED monitor — but with the added perk of USB connectivity. - HP Omen Transcend 32: Offers great USB-C connectivity and top-tier SDR image quality that make this 4K OLED monitor worth its high price. - Lenovo Legion R27fc-30: At less than $200, this is a good budget gaming monitor with a focus on motion clarity. - Acer Predator X32 X3: A great 4K OLED monitor that separates itself from the competition on two key points: connectivity and price. - Asus ProArt Display 5K: Not the best high-resolution display on the market, but it delivers a gorgeous 5K image and long list of features at a reasonable price. - Gigabyte G34WQCP: A $350 ultrawide that earns high marks in SDR brightness, contrast, and color performance. We test all monitors with a Datacolor Spyder X2 Ultra calibration tool. This tool can report objective measurements for brightness, contrast, color gamut, color accuracy, color temperature, gamma, and other metrics. Our results are recorded and compared to the results for past monitors. Though we rely on our eyes for initial impressions, comparing objective results lets us evaluate monitors against hundreds of older models from past reviews and testing. We examine motion clarity by quickly moving the camera across the map in Civilization VI, playing a round of Rocket League, and panning the camera across the landscape in Final Fantasy XIV—among other games. Finally, we use the popular UFO Test for an apples-to-apples comparison between displays. In addition to gaming prowess, we consider a monitor’s on-screen menu, ergonomic stand (or lack thereof), and overall build quality—all important qualities irrespective of use case. For more details, see our article on on how we test monitors at PCWorld. Who curated this article? Matthew S. Smith is a freelance technology journalist with 15 years of experience reviewing consumer electronics, including the universe of computer monitors. In addition to PCWorld, his work can be found on Wired, Digital Trends, Reviewed, Lifewire, and other technology publications. Gamers have unique needs that exceed an average user. Here’s what PC gamers should look for in a gaming monitor. Most widescreen gaming monitors have a resolution of 1920×1080 (1080p), 2560×1440 (1440p), or 4K (3840×2160). A higher resolution improves sharpness and clarity, which helps games look more detailed and lifelike. Increasing resolution also increases demand on your video card, however. Gamers with less powerful hardware may want to avoid 4K. A higher refresh leads to smoother motion by increasing the number of frames that can appear each second. It also reduces input lag, as each frame appears more quickly. A 144Hz refresh rate is a big improvement over the standard 60Hz, and 240Hz is better still. The improvement becomes more difficult to notice after 240Hz, but 360Hz monitors exist for those who want the lowest input lag possible. DisplayPort is the best connection for PC gaming. Even DisplayPort 1.4, which is rather old, can support 4K at 144Hz. HDMI 2.1 can handle 4K at 120Hz and is an acceptable connection for PC gaming, though most gamers will use it for a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S game console. What is the best gaming monitor? The best gaming monitor overall is the MSI MPG 341CQPX. The 34-inch panel joins a field of QD-OLED ultrawides, but stands out from the pack with better HDR, a 240Hz refresh rate, and USB-C port with 98 watts of Power Delivery. What is the best cheap gaming monitor? At less than $200, the Pixio PX248 Wave offers incredible value for gamers. The 1080p/200Hz monitor has all the essentials: good image quality, strong motion clarity, and Adaptive Sync support. What resolution is best for a gaming monitor? Many competitive gamers prefer 1080p resolution because it allows for high frame rates and low input lag even on modest hardware. This also makes it ideal for budget shoppers. 1080p is not as crisp as higher resolutions but, if it allows for higher frame rates, can look good in motion. 1440p remains a great mid-range option. It looks much sharper than 1080p but doesn’t drastically increase load on your video card. A variety of 1440p monitors now support a refresh rate up to 240Hz. 4K is the last word in sharpness and clarity. Playing a modern game on a 4K monitor takes the experience to a new level. It’s very demanding on your video card, however, so you’ll need top-tier hardware for a smooth experience. Ultrawide monitors differ in resolution because they have a wider screen. Most ultrawide monitors have a resolution of 3440×1440, which delivers sharpness similar to a 1440p ultrawide. Some larger monitors have more exotic resolutions: the 49-inch Samsung Odyssey G9 Neo, for example, has 5120×1440 resolution. Should I use AMD FreeSync or Nvidia G-Sync? AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync can synchronize the refresh rate of a compatible monitor with the output of an AMD or Nvidia video card. This ensures smooth motion and eliminates screen tearing, a distracting visual artifact. You might be surprised to learn that most AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync monitors rely on the VESA Adaptive Sync standard. This is why many gaming monitors now support both. The difference in performance is minimal. Should I buy an ultrawide gaming monitor? Our top choice, the Alienware AW3423DW, is an ultrawide gaming monitor. An ultrawide aspect ratio is more immersive in racing, simulation, and role-playing games. It also offers a large, more impressive perspective in many strategy games. Not all games support an ultrawide aspect ratio, however. It’s wise to check that your favorite games support ultrawide monitors before making a purchase. Consoles rarely support ultrawide aspect ratios, so console gamers should stick with a widescreen display.

You could also add a snazzy LCD screen (albeit not Corsair's $250 Xeneon), new RGB fans, or even an AIO cooler. Got a dusty old air cooler or a stock cooler that came with your CPU? If you want to upgrade your cooling, this is one of our very favorite air coolers for CPUs, with impressive heatsinks and fans. item.title: SALES: 10 Vacation Rentals Across North America For Your Next Family Reunion
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Family reunions can be stressful. There’s much to consider, from dealing with a motley of personalities to making sure the kids are looked after. But things get much easier when you land on the perfect vacation rental, one in a crowd-pleasing location, with a spacious layout and plenty of amenities that will keep everyone happy. Whether you’re bringing the gang together for an outdoor adventure at Yosemite National Park, or seeking a laid-back sojourn in the Caribbean, the rentals on this list satisfy every kind of trip. Each featuring four bedrooms or more, these properties are sure to fit the entire clan with luxe amenities worth traveling for: think saltwater pools, golf simulators, and private beach access. What’s more, many are within the top 1% of guest reviews in their area, which means they’re loved by the people who have visited (and are often booked for return trips). Below, the best vacation rentals for family reunions across North America. We've selected these listings based on ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. Why we love it: Private pool, proximity to beach, game roomJust steps away from Alys Beach, located on Scenic Highway 30A, this sunny and spacious six-bedroom home was designed for families: four king bedrooms with en suite bathrooms (one of which houses two extra twin beds); a bunk room with a double and four additional twin beds; and a queen with a trundle. There’s a game room, complete with ping-pong and Foosball tables, plus large-screen TVs. The little ones can enjoy amenities too, like mini cribs and pack-and-plays. If the family would rather swim at home, there’s a gorgeous heated pool for everyone to wade in, with sun loungers, an adjacent barbecue, and even a little tanning ledge for kids to take their first steps in the water. Location: Inlet Beach, Florida Things to do nearby: Seacrest Beach, Deer Lake State Park, Alys Beach Why we love it: Study area, in-unit washer/dryer, outdoor patioNantucket, with its pristine beaches and vibrant historic town, makes for an excellent family gathering. This classic, cedar-shingled home features an abundance of windows that bring in natural light, spotless interiors, and plainly chic furnishings. There are five bedrooms with high ceilings (some offer glimpses of the harbor), four full bathrooms, and a spacious kitchen. On the first floor, French doors open out to an outdoor entertainment area, with sectional seating, a dining table that seats 10, a gas grill, and an outdoor shower, all enclosed by a landscaped lawn—the perfect place for the group to kick back and relax. Location: Nantucket, Massachusetts Things to do nearby: Nantucket Atheneum, Quaker Meeting House, Children's Beach Why we love it: Hot tub, proximity to ski resorts, golf simulatorThis dreamy A-frame home in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands offers adventurous family members proximity to the slopes at Hidden Valley and Seven Springs resorts. With seven bedrooms spread across three floors, there’s enough space for 20 guests to spread out, plus a fully equipped kitchen, dedicated theater area, game room, and even a golf simulator. After a long day of activities, there’s no better place to relax tired muscles than the hot tub outside, fit for six, or the firepit, surrounded by cozy loungers. Keep in mind the area does get icy over the winter, so 4WD is recommended. Location: Somerset, Pennsylvania Things to do nearby: Hidden Valley Resort, Seven Springs Mountain Resort, Ohiopyle State Park Why we love it: Gazebo, valley views, fireplaceLocated in the heart of Ohio’s Amish country, Hillside Villa is a bucolic escape for the extended family. While the entire villa can be booked (check for availability on the “Premier House” option), you can also opt for individual units, from a deluxe room for two with a jetted hot tub to a junior room that sleeps up to four. Each comes with scenic views of the hills, along with shared kitchen access (coffee and tea maker provided). There are 55-inch flat-screen TVs too, along with features like fireplaces and porches. In the backyard, you’ll find a gazebo with a firepit, perfect for watching the sunset descend over the farm-filled valley. Location: Millersburg, Ohio Things to do nearby: Country Acres Mini Golf, Pro Football Hall of Fame, Belden Village Mall Why we love it: Contemporary interior design, private lake access, barbecueOffering 200 feet of private lakefront in Austin, this modern four-bedroom is a rare retreat. Ideal for a multigenerational family, it’s composed of a main house with two king bedrooms and a guesthouse with a king bedroom, plus a large bunk room with eight twin beds. Spend your days gliding along the lake on a kayak or paddleboard, floating on the 16-foot lily pad, or taking a hike through the surrounding Balcones Canyonland Preserve. End the fun on the two-story party dock, where you can enjoy a meal outside, with s’mores for dessert around the firepit. Location: Austin, Texas Things to do nearby: Lake Austin, Sixth Street, University of Texas at Austin Why we love it: Hiking trail access, pool table, forest viewsThis Yosemite home, with its breathtaking cathedral windows and stone fireplace, will offer the family a stay they won’t forget. The perfect place to retreat to after a day spent at Yosemite National Park, this four-bedroom is wonderfully western, with its hanging deer antlers, wooden furniture, and tons of colorful textiles. Your group can spread out between two queen beds, two twin beds, and two bunk beds (one with a trundle). Prepare meals in the fully equipped kitchen, then enjoy some family time at the dining table, which seats up to 10. Up in the loft, you’ll find a mini arcade, a number of board games, and a pool table. Location: Yosemite National Park, California Things to do nearby: Yosemite National Park, Yosemite Valley, Yosemite Arch Rock Gate Entrance Why we love it: Mountain views, gym, wildlife sightingsCozy, inviting, and lived-in, this Jackson Hole property is the ultimate mountain escape. Located in Spring Creek Ranch, the home is in a 1,000-acre ranch community, perched atop East Gros Ventre Butte, 800 feet above the valley floor. The first thing you’ll notice upon walking in is a kitchen and dining area that flows into the living room, with large windows overlooking the mountains. There are four bedrooms (three kings and one with two twin beds), each with views of the Tetons. Poke around the woods, watch a movie around the fireplace, and look out for elk. Location: Jackson, Wyoming Things to do nearby: Jackson Hole Valley, Jackson Hole Wildlife Safaris, Jackson Town Square Why we love it: Scenic views, in-unit washer/dryer, beach accessIn Quebec City, the Saguenay Fjord stretches over 62 miles and is surrounded by dramatic granite cliffs. This charming, four-bedroom home will place you right in front of the action. Settle back on the front porch with your loved ones and watch the tides roll in, or take sunset walks along the beach. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need for meals at home, while the grand dining table looks out into the water. Outside, there’s a swing for little ones, plus a few Adirondack chairs for the adults to continue savoring the view. Location: Saguenay, Quebec City, Canada Things to do nearby: Saguenay River, Theatre du Palais Municipal, Okwari Le Fjord Why we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, chef available upon request, beach accessDreaming of a family reunion across the border? At this bungalow in Placencia, Belize, you’ll have the Caribbean Sea right at your doorstep. Ideal for two families, the four bedrooms (one king and three queens) are spread out in such a way that two of them have their own separate entrance. Spend your days soaking up the sun, swimming in the saltwater pool, gliding along the water on a stand-up paddleboard, or preparing a fresh lunch in the outdoor kitchen. And if you truly want to leave your worries at the door, in-house chef services are available upon request. Location: Placencia, Mexico Things to do nearby: Placencia Beach, Placencia Pier, Maya Beach Why we love it: Panoramic windows, hot tub, in-unit washer/dryerFor extra-large families with great taste, this eight-bedroom beach house is a no-brainer, with jaw-dropping, panoramic views of Lake Michigan and plenty of luxe amenities, from a hot tub and game room to a heated pool. There are gorgeous design details throughout, like vaulted wooden ceilings and circular ship-style windows. Rooms are split between the main house and guest house, with two separate kitchens. Just an 11-minute walk from Saugatuck Dunes State Park, the house provides access to endless scenic trails. Bonus: It’s pet-friendly too. Location: Saugatuck, Michigan Things to do nearby: Kalamazoo River, Saugatuck Dunes State Park, Oval Beach This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: SALES: A secret hideaway on Australia's wildest coast
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
Champagne, crocs and no roads: The secret luxury hideaway on Australia's wildest coast Accessible only by sea or air, this remote retreat pairs five-star luxury with ancient rock art, spectacular gorges and extraordinary isolation. For most of the 80-minute charter flight from Darwin, there is nothing beneath me but the Timor Sea. There are no roads to where I'm going. Nor are there towns, settlements or shops. Then, suddenly, Australia reappears. The endless expanse of blue gives way to pale sandbars and braided waterways, then rust-red rock, mangroves and a serpentine river slicing its way through the landscape. Our Cessna banks towards a long red-dirt airstrip carved into the bush. As I duck through the plane's tiny doorway, I'm hit by a wall of hot, dusty air. Then someone takes my bag and hands me a glass of Bollinger. This is Berkeley River Lodge, an off-grid luxury retreat on one of Australia's most inaccessible coasts. Five-star luxury, 200km from the nearest road I've travelled extensively across Australia, but I've never been anywhere that feels quite this remote. Berkeley River Lodge lies in the north-east of Western Australia's Kimberley region, a far-flung wilderness of sandstone escarpments, river gorges and empty beaches. From the airstrip, red earth and green scrub stretch to the horizon. Beyond the lodge, this vast stretch of coastline is virtually uninhabited. In a world where even far-flung destinations are increasingly within reach, this still feels completely off the map. "If I dropped you out there and let you go for a walk, you would walk somewhere no [guest] has likely ever walked before," lodge guide Josh Halloran tells me later. My five flight companions and I are ushered into an open-air safari buggy, our luggage already stowed. As we drive from the airstrip and crest a small hill, the lodge comes into view: 15 villas perched on sand dunes, linked by winding red-sand tracks and tethered by a main lodge, its brilliantly blue swimming pool looking decidedly out of place. As we get closer, I see a flurry of uniformed staff waiting for us to arrive. Nothing about the landscape outside suggests any of this should be here. The price is almost as startling as the location. A compulsory five-night, all-inclusive stay costs A$19,750 (£10,370/US$13,870) for two people. It's an extraordinary amount of money to spend travelling to a place with almost nothing around it. But as I quickly learn, that is precisely the point. On paper, Berkeley River Lodge doesn't really make sense. Only open for four months each year, it offers morning yoga on the deck, evening cocktails and multi-course tasting menus. There's a maximum of 30 guests at a time, with 22 staff to cater to their every whim. Yet there's no mains power or water, no mobile phone reception and, crucially, no road in or out. Although the sea is tantalisingly close, swimming is strictly off limits; this is saltwater crocodile country. "The nearest road is over 200km [124 miles] away," says co-owner Rachel Bromage, explaining that the only way to reach the lodge is by air or boat. "Lots of the Kimberley is remote, but this is truly remote." For guest Rob Wheeldon-Fookes, who has come here on honeymoon with his new wife Liz, the absence of almost everything is part of the appeal. "I love the idea of being cut off," he says. "There's something very luxurious about being away from other people." It's surreal encountering civilisation in a place this wild. At the lodge entrance, a board cheerily lists the day's adventures, from barramundi fishing and river cruises to beach drives and bushwalks. I'm shown to my villa, an airy, understated space with timber floors, a huge bed dressed in crisp white linen and floor-to-ceiling glass doors opening onto a private deck. In the open-air bathroom, a freestanding marble tub sits beneath the vast Kimberley skies. Later that night, I lie back and gaze up at the luminous sweep of the Milky Way, soundtracked by the ocean and a chorus of fat frogs. A landscape billions of years in the making The next morning, I'm aboard a boat, speeding up the Berkeley River into Casuarina Creek with a small group of guests. The waters are hemmed in by towering cliffs of rust-red sandstone, their enormous, striated blocks stacked like Jenga pieces. Halloran warns us against taking a dip. "You wouldn't want to enter the water here. There's big things that live in there." Instead, we head ashore and clamber up a steep slope of loose rocks, slipping and scrambling in the relentless heat. Halloran, who spends much of the hike barefoot, bounds ahead, stopping occasionally to point out things we'd otherwise miss: hundreds of tiny white shells carefully collected by a male bowerbird to attract a mate, trees whose bark can be used to carry water, a giant rock with the ripples of an ancient waterway seemingly frozen into its surface. This is an almost incomprehensibly old place, with rock formations dating back around 1.8 billion years, long before complex animal life evolved. Plan your trip: Getting there: Berkeley River Lodge is accessible via an 80-minute scenic charter flight from Darwin. When to visit: The lodge is open from 1 May to 31 August. Its 15 villas accommodate a maximum of 30 guests. Cost: Five-night, all-inclusive packages for the 2027 season cost A$19,750 (£10,370/US$13,870) for two people sharing, or A$18,250 (£9,545/US$12,825) for single occupancy. The price includes return charter flights from Darwin, accommodation, gourmet dining and beverages, one in-villa spa treatment per person and guided excursions. What to do: Included activities include river cruises, guided hikes to ancient Aboriginal rock art, barramundi fishing and sunset 4WD beach excursions. New for 2027 are a Kimberley botanicals masterclass and a barefoot barbecue experience. From the top, we gaze down into a spectacular gorge, its sheer cliffs plunging towards a ribbon of green water. I shuffle to the edge of the escarpment, slightly terrified by the vertical drop below me, and see a crocodile's tail poking out from the base of a waterfall. When Halloran later invites us to swim in a separate, pandanus-fringed waterhole, I decline, still unnerved by the croc sighting, though quickly regret it as I watch other guests float past on their backs like otters. Eventually, Halloran leads us into a rocky overhang where he points to a series of faded ochre drawings. We're on Balanggarra Country, and the rock art offers a glimpse into the region's long Aboriginal history. Among the drawings is an animal that he says could be an extinct thylacine – a wolf-like marsupial once found across Australia. I gaze at depictions of slender human figures with elaborate headdresses and tassels hanging from their bodies, examples of the mysterious 12,000-year-old Gwion Gwion rock art, sometimes known as Bradshaw paintings. Halloran suspects there is much more ancient art scattered across this vast landscape, still waiting to be found. "Do you realise where you are?" he asks. "One of the most remote places in the world." Back at the lodge, a five-course dinner appears as effortlessly as if we were sitting in a city restaurant. Seated around a long table overlooking the tidal flats, with white linen and rows of wine glasses, we're served a wine-paired feast: duck rillettes, vitello tonnato, charred asparagus with miso hollandaise and wagyu sirloin. The meal ends with an elaborate creation of chocolate, cashew and tonka foam. Behind the scenes, however, delivering this level of luxury requires extraordinary planning. The lodge operates entirely off grid, generating its own electricity and drawing water from a bore beneath the dunes. Fresh produce arrives on twice weekly flights, while larger supplies come by barge every 10 to 12 weeks. "If you're out of lemons, you're not going to get any more lemons," general manager Hannah Wark, tells me, laughing. And when things go wrong, it's not always as simple as a missing ingredient. Wark has dealt with bushfires, torrential rain and medical scares serious enough to involve the Royal Flying Doctor Service. With no hospital or road access, an emergency can require an evacuation by air. But nothing could have prepared them for November 2025, when Cyclone Fina struck with devastating force. As the category-three cyclone's winds howled across the coast, two caretakers stationed at the lodge during the wet season took refuge in an underground bunker, emerging some 18 hours later. "It's like a bomb's gone off. It's apocalyptic," they told Bromage over satellite phone. The lodge wasn't insured and the owners faced a difficult decision: walk away or attempt to rebuild in time for the next season, just five months away. Remarkably, Berkeley River Lodge reopened in May 2026, just in time for the first guests of the season. Its villas and public spaces have been extensively refurbished, though diesel generators have temporarily replaced the solar power system destroyed in the cyclone, which is expected to be restored in 2027. "Anything that could move has been replaced. Every cushion, every side table, every chair. Every sun lounge," said Bromage. There was even a snake discovered inside the staff pool table. "The Kimberley's the boss here; it's in control," Bromage said. Despite – or perhaps thanks to – the isolation, there's a surprisingly sociable side to life at Berkeley River Lodge. With no TVs in the rooms, and everyone rotating through excursions and evening meals, strangers quickly become friends. Wark says guests often arrive at the airport in Darwin having never met, only to leave planning future trips together. "Some have already booked other holidays with each other before they even leave the property," she says. And while the lodge's comforts are considerable, it's the surrounding emptiness that seems to make the deepest impression. "It's so easy just to walk away and have complete silence," says Liz, the honeymooner I met at breakfast. "You get a complete vista of the ocean with nothing there. No boats. No people... absolutely nothing but nature." On our final evening, we're treated to a new barbecue experience the lodge plans to offer next season. At a sandy spot behind one of the villas, a long table has been set up in the sand, with lights strung overhead. As the last of the sunlight fades over the Kimberley, we're served heaping platters of chargrilled ribeye, honey-glazed carrots and grilled radicchio followed by flamed pineapple with macadamia crumble. There's a celebratory mood in the air. We're the last guests of the season, and tomorrow, almost as soon as our plane takes off, the staff will begin the enormous task of packing the lodge up for cyclone season before they leave soon after. A few days ago, we were strangers climbing aboard a tiny plane in Darwin; now we're swapping stories and bonding over our adventures. Tomorrow, we'll return to a world of roads, traffic and mobile phone reception. For now, though, sitting barefoot in the sand, hours from the nearest town, I find myself wishing the whole experience could start again. "It still gives me goosebumps," Bromage tells me.
